name: Molima, Tola'ai dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Engkvist, Leif & Helena Engkvist. 1992 [updated June 2002]. Organized Phonology Data of Molima Language (Tola'ai dialect). Ms., SIL, Ukarumpa, Papua New Guinea. 6 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 42273 'Molima Organised Phonology Data' (consultant-checked by Kim Blewett, accepted 10/12/92).
catalog_locator: Sec. 5 'Suprasegmentals', p. 2; saved file See also sec. 6 p. 3 (penultimate stress marked in bold) and sec. 7 p. 4 (non-syllabic /u/, /i/ do not carry stress).
catalog_quote: There are no tones in the language. There are no long vowels- we have found one contrasting word with two identical vowels where the two vowels have two pulses, ['gaana] 'gill' (not ['ga:na]), ['gana] 'circle of stones'. There are a few words which have two identical vowels following each other. The pronunciation is not a lengthened vowel, but two identical vowels with each its own puls. The phonemic representation is /gahana/ 'gill', /vihila/ 'run', /mahalaya/ 'heaven'. Stress occur on penultimate syllable except in some words ending with vowel /a/ where the stress is on antepenultimate syllable, e.g. ['bunama] /bunama/ 'oil', ['imula] /imula/ 'island'. I think the underlying form is penultimate stress for words like these also. You may explain it as these words end with a closed syllable and the [a] is an epenthetic vowel.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable. A small set of /a/-final words surface with antepenultimate stress (e.g. 'bunama 'oil', 'imula 'island'); the authors treat these as underlyingly penultimate, the final [a] being epenthetic after a closed syllable (/bu.nam.a/, /i.mul.a/). Non-syllabic /u/ and /i/ (glides before vowels) never carry stress (sec. 7). No tone, no contrastive length.
new_statements.exceptions: Some words ending in /a/ have antepenultimate surface stress (['bunama] 'oil', ['imula] 'island'), analysed as penultimate over an underlying closed syllable plus epenthetic [a]. Sec. 6 notes the syllable analysis of vowel sequences is 'still very uncertain', which affects syllable counting for stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement on citation forms in an SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet; Tola'ai dialect. Stress not written in the orthography.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes the Tola'ai dialect of Molima (moli1248; Glottolog lists no sub-dialect codes; Wikipedia/Ethnologue dialects Tola'ai, Ai'alu, Tosila'ai). Its orthography chart (p. 6) also covers neighbouring varieties (Iamalele, Minaveha, Gumawana, Dobu) but the stress statement is for Tola'ai Molima only. Fagululu, listed by Glottolog as an alternate name, is treated by Lithgow 1976 (para 20) as a separate lect near Yamalele.
